rejected.title: Comparative anatomy
card: Comparative anatomy compares the body structures of different species. Similar structures can be evidence that species are related.
Homologous structure
a structure with the same basic design and origin in different species, but which may do different jobs. The forelimbs of a human, a bat and a whale are an example.
Vestigial structure
a structure that has lost most or all of its original use. The tiny hip bones in a whale are an example.
Homologous structures suggest the species inherited the structure from a common ancestor. Vestigial structures suggest the ancestor used the structure and its descendants no longer need it.
rejected.remember: Homologous means shared origin, even if the job differs. Vestigial means the use has been lost.

a.q: A bat's wing and a horse's foreleg have the same bone layout but are used for flying and running. What are these structures?
opts: Homologous structures, showing a common ancestor
Vestigial structures, showing a lost function
Homologous structures, showing the same function
Vestigial structures, showing a common ancestor
a.why: The bones share the same basic design despite different jobs, so they are homologous and point to a common ancestor. They are not vestigial, because both limbs are still used.
a.clue: Look at the bone layout, not at the job each limb does.

b.q: Pythons have tiny hip and thigh bones under the skin, ending in small claw-like spurs used in courtship. Lizards have full hip and leg bones used for walking. What do the python's bones best suggest?
opts: Pythons and lizards share an ancestor that had working legs
Pythons are slowly evolving working legs to walk again
The bones are not vestigial, as the spurs still have a use
Pythons and lizards use these leg bones for the same job
b.why: The python's leg bones have lost most of their original use in walking, so they are vestigial, and they match the leg bones of lizards. This suggests both groups descend from an ancestor with working legs. The spurs do not stop the bones being vestigial, because a vestigial structure can keep a small part of its use.
b.clue: A vestigial structure has lost most or all of its use, not always every bit.

b.q: Some snakes have tiny leg bones buried in their bodies that serve no purpose. Their lizard-like ancestors used legs to walk. What does this suggest?
opts: The bones are vestigial, left from a walking ancestor
The bones are homologous to wings, so snakes can fly
The bones are vestigial, so snakes never had ancestors
The bones are homologous, as they have the same function
b.why: The leg bones have lost their use, so they are vestigial, and they suggest snakes descended from ancestors that walked. The tempting homologous option fails because the bones no longer share a function.
b.clue: Ask whether the bones still do a job.

a.best: Homologous structures, showing a common ancestor

b.best: The bones are vestigial, left from a walking ancestor

problems.detail: Why (b) says the homologous option fails 'because the bones no longer share a function'. This implies homologous structures must share a function, which contradicts the card: homologous structures may do different jobs. The option fails because it wrongly claims the bones have the same function, and snake leg bones are in fact homologous to lizard legs as well as vestigial.

Two distractors are absurd for Year 12 ('snakes never had ancestors', 'snakes can fly'). The stem also states 'serve no purpose' and 'ancestors used legs to walk', which the right option echoes, so the answer can be picked without understanding the idea.

'Serve no purpose' is too absolute. In pythons and boas the leg remnants form pelvic spurs used in courtship and combat. The card's own wording, 'lost most or all of its original use', would be safer.
